passage.title: Deep-Sea Mining and the Limits of Regulation

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Four kilometres beneath the central Pacific, between Hawaii and Mexico, an abyssal plain called the Clarion-Clipperton Zone (CCZ) is littered with dark, potato-sized rocks. These are polymetallic nodules, formed over millions of years as dissolved metals accumulate around fragments of shell or bone, and they now sit at the centre of a divisive international debate. The nodules are rich in the metals battery manufacturers require: roughly 25 to 30 per cent manganese, 1 to 2 per cent each of nickel and copper, and 0.2 to 0.3 per cent cobalt. The United States Geological Survey estimates that the zone holds more than 21 billion dry tonnes of nodules, possibly more cobalt and manganese than all known land reserves combined. This abundance explains the new interest in the seabed as a source of critical minerals.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Who may extract these minerals is decided by the International Seabed Authority (ISA), a United Nations body in Kingston, Jamaica that administers the seabed beyond national jurisdiction. Its 172 members met in July 2026 for their 31st annual session, but again closed without agreement on the Mining Code, the rules that would govern commercial extraction. Negotiations stall repeatedly over the same questions: how much environmental data is sufficient, who would pay for damage, whether permits should wait for a moratorium, and how royalties would be shared. By the close of the Assembly, 46 countries, over a quarter of members, had called for a moratorium or precautionary pause. Exploration contracts now cover roughly 1.5 million square kilometres of the CCZ, yet a Vanuatu proposal to create a mechanism for identifying gaps in scientific knowledge was not adopted, and talks will not resume until March 2027.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Supporters of extraction point to the pressure of demand. Around 70 per cent of the world's cobalt is mined in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, about 60 per cent of nickel comes from Indonesia, and China refines roughly 90 per cent of global cobalt and nickel capacity. Advocates argue that ocean-floor recovery would diversify these supply chains and carry a smaller footprint than some land mines; one developer claims that producing a kilogram of nickel from nodules emits about 6.2 kilograms of carbon dioxide, against 20 to 100 kilograms for conventional mining. Critics reply that such figures ignore the energy used in processing and transport, and that even a mature nodule industry would satisfy only a fraction of the projected supply gap.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The most frequently cited obstacle is the gap between exploration and ecological knowledge. A 2023 checklist in the journal Current Biology, compiled by researchers at the Natural History Museum in London, recorded 5,578 species from CCZ samples, but only 436 had formal scientific names, leaving roughly 92 per cent of recorded species undescribed; the true total may be between 6,000 and 8,000 species. A review published in 2026 by the same museum and the National Oceanography Centre examined fifty years of mining tests. It found that geophysical scars persist for decades: tracks left by a 1979 trial were still visible 44 years later, and although small, mobile animals recolonised some areas within months, few communities had returned to undisturbed conditions even two decades on.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Scientists judge the danger greater still at the two other target habitats: seafloor massive sulphides around hydrothermal vents, and cobalt-rich crusts on seamounts. Vent animals depend entirely on the chemistry their vents produce, so crushing a vent removes their only home. In July 2026 the International Union for Conservation of Nature updated its Red List, classifying 125 of the 201 known vent-dwelling mollusc species as threatened, about 62 per cent of the total. Data from the CCZ are equally sobering: in the largest trial so far, which removed 3,000 tonnes of nodules at a depth of 4,280 metres, macrofaunal density fell by 37 per cent and species richness by 32 per cent within two years. The 2026 review concludes that major disturbance at active vents and seamounts would not be compatible with the biodiversity policies most governments have signed.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: National positions remain deeply split. France, Germany, the United Kingdom and Canada support a moratorium, while the United States, which never ratified the Law of the Sea treaty, has proposed leasing seabed areas near American Samoa. China is expanding its exploration programme and India is seeking more licences. Two wealthy economies illustrate the divergence. Norway, which opened part of its Arctic shelf in 2024, agreed in December 2025 to issue no licences during the current parliamentary term, postponing its first round until at least 2029. Japan, by contrast, reported in February 2026 that its drilling vessel Chikyu had recovered rare-earth-bearing mud from about 6,000 metres near the island of Minamitorishima, and a larger trial is planned for 2027.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The industry has also divided Pacific neighbours. Nauru, the Cook Islands, Tonga and Kiribati see seabed minerals as a route to economic diversification and sponsor exploration in the CCZ, whereas Palau, Fiji and Vanuatu have joined the calls for a pause, citing the ocean's central place in their culture and economies. Africa has shifted too: six countries, among them Mauritius and Mozambique, now back a precautionary pause. Some researchers argue that recycling deserves a larger role, since much already-extracted metal remains locked in discarded products. With the ISA unable to set a timeline and baselines still incomplete, the future of the deep seabed and the species that depend on it will be settled only when negotiations resume in 2027.
